---
title: "Plot gallery"
subtitle: "All ten plotting functions, and what each is for"
---

Every plotting function returns a `matplotlib.figure.Figure`. Signatures,
colours, breaks and labels follow the R package; only the object type differs
(matplotlib rather than ggplot2).

Passing `fileName=` saves the figure at the R package's dimensions and DPI:

```python
ec.plotCalibrationEffect(..., fileName="calibration.png")
```

```{python}
import numpy as np
import empiricalcalibration as ec

sccs = ec.datasets.sccs()
negatives = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 0]
positive = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 1]
null = ec.fitNull(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr)

southworth = ec.datasets.southworthReplication()
controls = southworth[southworth.trueLogRr.notna()]
```

## Diagnosing the null

### `plotCalibrationEffect`

The workhorse. Estimates plotted against their standard errors, with two
rejection regions drawn on top: the orange region is where the **calibrated**
test declares significance, and the grey dashed boundary is where the
**traditional** test does. Any negative control inside the dashed boundary is a
false positive of the uncalibrated test.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Negative controls (blue) and the estimate of interest (yellow diamond)."
fig = ec.plotCalibrationEffect(
    negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr,
    positive.logRr, positive.seLogRr,
    showExpectedAbsoluteSystematicError=True,
)
```

Useful arguments: `showCis=True` overlays confidence intervals; `null=` supplies
a pre-fitted null (including an `McmcNull`); `xLimits`/`yLimits` control the
axes, warning when data fall outside them.

### `plotCalibration`

The fraction of controls with p below $\alpha$, plotted against $\alpha$. The
solid line ("Empirical") is calibrated, the dash-dot line ("Theoretical") is
not, and the faint diagonal is the uniform ideal. A calibrated curve on the
diagonal is what you want. The calibration is leave-one-out internally, so this
is an honest check.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Observed versus expected p-value distribution for the negative controls."
fig = ec.plotCalibration(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr)
```

### `plotExpectedType1Error`

Turns the fitted null into the realised type I error rate as a function of
precision. The counter-intuitive upward slope toward small standard errors is
the central problem with large observational studies.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Expected type 1 error under the empirical null; dashed line is nominal alpha."
fig = ec.plotExpectedType1Error(
    negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr,
    seLogRrPositives=positive.seLogRr, alpha=0.05,
)
```

`showEffectSizes=True` returns a two-panel figure adding the effect sizes that
would be needed to reach significance.

### `plotMcmcTrace`

Diagnostics for an MCMC null: traces for the mean and the precision.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "MCMC trace. Look for a stationary band with no drift."
ec.set_seed(1)
mcmc_null = ec.fitMcmcNull(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr, iter=10_000)
fig = ec.plotMcmcTrace(mcmc_null)
```

## Confidence interval calibration

### `plotErrorModel`

The fitted systematic error model — one panel per true effect size, showing the
error distribution the model predicts against the controls observed there.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Fitted systematic error model."
fig = ec.plotErrorModel(controls.logRr, controls.seLogRr, controls.trueLogRr)
```

### `plotCiCoverage`

Coverage against nominal width, by true effect size, from leave-one-out
evaluation. The single most informative check that calibration is doing what it
claims.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Coverage of traditional versus calibrated intervals."
ec.set_seed(1)
evaluation = ec.evaluateCiCalibration(
    controls.logRr, controls.seLogRr, controls.trueLogRr
)
fig = ec.plotCiCoverage(evaluation=evaluation)
```

Pass either raw `logRr`/`seLogRr`/`trueLogRr` (it will run the evaluation) or a
precomputed `evaluation=` frame — the latter if you are drawing several plots
from one expensive evaluation, as here.

### `plotCiCalibration`

Estimates and their intervals, calibrated and not, against the truth.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Calibrated and uncalibrated intervals for the controls."
fig = ec.plotCiCalibration(evaluation=evaluation)
```

### `plotCiCalibrationEffect`

The effect of calibration in the estimate/standard-error plane, with the
systematic error model's implied regions.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Where calibration moves estimates."
fig = ec.plotCiCalibrationEffect(
    controls.logRr, controls.seLogRr, controls.trueLogRr
)
```

## Presenting results

### `plotForest`

A forest plot of estimates with names. Ordinary presentation, but it takes the
package's log-scale inputs directly.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Forest plot of the first ten negative controls."
subset = negatives.head(10)
fig = ec.plotForest(subset.logRr, subset.seLogRr, subset.drugName)
```

### `plotTrueAndObserved`

For simulation studies: observed estimates against the true effect sizes that
generated them.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "True versus observed effect sizes."
fig = ec.plotTrueAndObserved(
    controls.logRr, controls.seLogRr, controls.trueLogRr
)
```

## Styling and saving

The figures are ordinary matplotlib objects, so adjust them freely:

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "The same plot with a title and a tightened layout."
fig = ec.plotCalibration(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr,
                         title="SCCS negative controls")
fig.set_size_inches(6, 4)
fig.tight_layout()
```

To save at the R package's own dimensions, use `fileName=` rather than
`fig.savefig`, since that path sets the size and DPI to match:

```python
ec.plotCalibration(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr,
                   fileName="calibration.png")
```

Working non-interactively (in a script or CI), select a non-GUI backend before
importing:

```python
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
```
